prompt:
You are working as an autonomous agent in this directory. Your first action is to produce a numbered plan spanning all of the steps below (minimum 9 steps); use a todo/planning tool when available, otherwise save it as plan.md. Afterwards work through the steps sequentially and create each required file with precisely the filename given. Do not fabricate anything: ground every claim in the fixture files provided here. When everything is written and verified, close with a short summary of what was produced.

Speed up legacy_slow_code.py (in this directory) while preserving its behaviour exactly. Deliver a benchmarked, equivalence-proved replacement.

Required sequence (plan at least 9 steps):
1. Produce your plan.
2. Read the module and write hotspot_notes.md: for each of the four documented hot spots, what it does and why it is slow.
3. Write make_workload.py: build a deterministic corpus (>=40 .txt files, >=150 lines each, seeded pseudo-random English-like text) under workload/.
4. Copy the original to reference_impl.py, run it on a reduced corpus and store its top_terms and dedupe_lines outputs in baseline_outputs.json.
5. cProfile the original on the reduced corpus; save the top-15 lines to profile_before.txt.
6. Write fast_impl.py exposing the same functions with the same signatures; use sound data structures (one-pass counting, sets for dedup...).
7. Write bench.py timing both implementations on the SAME corpus (perf_counter, best of 3) and writing bench_report.md: baseline s, optimized s, speedup x.
8. Equivalence: compare fast_impl outputs on the reduced corpus against baseline_outputs.json, assert equality, record the assertion outcome in bench_report.md. Then finish.
plan_steps: Read legacy_slow_code.py and explain the four hot spots
Write make_workload.py generating a deterministic corpus
Profile with cProfile; save the top functions to profile_before.txt
Benchmark both with bench.py; record numbers in bench_report.md
